# Event-driven device discovery architecture ## Public ownership boundary manager watch creates a producer; monitor watch subscribes to an existing one. `YubiKeyManager.Find…Async` delegates to `YubiKeyDiscovery`, which creates a fresh scoped finder per call and retires its read scope in `finally`. It neither starts tracking nor publishes into a monitor. `YubiKeyManager.WatchAsync(ct)` creates and disposes a private monitor per enumeration, starting on the first `MoveNextAsync`. `CreateMonitorAsync(ct)` returns an initialized monitor for the caller to share and dispose. Every monitor scans all interfaces, even without subscribers. Build membership projections from replay, or call `FindAllAsync` for a one-off. Live Management reads remain the configuration API. ## Components and scan flow | Component | Responsibility | |---|---| | `HotplugSignals` | Starts optional `IDeviceChangeListener` implementations; owns their teardown and a capacity-one signal channel | | `RescanScheduler` | Uses `TimeProvider` for initial, interval, and coalesced hotplug triggers | | `YubiKeyMonitor` | Composes resources; runs the sole sequential discovery/publication loop; owns lifetime | | `IMonitoredDiscovery` / `FindYubiKeys` | Invalidates evidence, scans with discovery budgets, retires read scopes | | `DeviceChangeFeed` | Holds membership and revision; publishes diffs and manages isolated subscriptions | | `SnapshotDiff` | Computes identity retention, replacements, and metadata updates | ```text platform listener Changed callback → HotplugSignals: capacity-one Channel, DropWrite → RescanScheduler: Initial, Interval, or Hotplug(transports) → monitor loop: invalidate evidence for Hotplug, await discovery → DeviceChangeFeed.Apply: SnapshotDiff, then atomic publication → independent bounded subscriber buffers → Subscribe: captured replay → SnapshotComplete → live tail ``` The scheduler yields `Initial` immediately. It then waits for a signal or the five-second fallback interval. Hotplug hints are coalesced with a 200 ms quiet window and a one-second cap. The cap bounds coalescing, not scan completion or detection latency. Each consumed hint combines transport flags; when the capacity-one channel is full, extra hints are dropped rather than queued. This is safe because any hotplug trigger invalidates evidence globally and the next scan reconciles all interfaces. Hints received during a scan can request a follow-up scan. Elapsed-time checks prevent a continuously refilled channel from starving the coalescing deadline. Scheduler timing is tested with `FakeTimeProvider`. The monitor awaits every scan and its publication before requesting the next trigger. Immediately before a hotplug scan it calls `IMonitoredDiscovery.InvalidateEvidence(transports)`. Listener callbacks only signal; they do not invalidate evidence themselves. The monitor has no lock or parallel producer. `FindYubiKeys` still serializes its own scan callers with a semaphore. ## Discovery budgets and partial results `DiscoveryBudgets` centralizes the enumeration budget (five seconds; Linux scans that overlap a `pcscd` restart measured under 300 ms), identity-read budget (two seconds per attempt), and metadata-read budget (three seconds). Identity reads can retry up to three attempts; concurrent finder callers can queue on the scan lock. `ScanUpperBound` is a sum of stage budgets, **not a hard end-to-end wall-clock guarantee**. `EnumerateInterfacesAsync` starts both in-scope transport waits together. If enumeration exceeds its budget, the behaviour depends on the caller. One-shot `Find…Async` logs a warning, omits that transport for this call and returns the other transport's results. The monitor's path (`IMonitoredDiscovery.FindAllAsync`) throws `TimeoutException` instead, because a partial scan diffed against the previous snapshot would read as removals of every key on the stalled transport; the loop logs and retries on the next trigger, and the previous snapshot stands. Caller cancellation abandons the wait. Late enumeration completion/failure is observed and logged at Debug level; it does not add interfaces to an already published scan. Budgets bound callers' waits, not native execution or ownership. Already-dispatched work completes and cleans up independently. A returned initialized monitor is not proof that every transport or metadata field was accessible. The monitor can reuse successful serial-less metadata. Its identity cache checks Product ID changes; its metadata cache currently does not perform that same check. Listener invalidation and observed absence still evict both. Treat cached metadata as last-known evidence rather than a periodic live read. ## Snapshot diff rules `SnapshotDiff.Apply(current, observed, revision)` builds a successor dictionary keyed by the physical interface-path set (`YubiKeyDevice.PhysicalIdentityKeyFor`), not `DeviceId` or the current evidence tier. - An absent identity produces `DeviceRemoved`; a new identity produces `DeviceAdded`. - A changed connection set, or two known serials that contradict each other, produces removal of the predecessor followed by addition of the successor. Unknown serials do not prove substitution. - Otherwise, the originally published object is retained, so its later removal correlates by reference. - For retained `YubiKeyDevice` objects, changed non-null `DeviceInfo` replaces last-known metadata and produces `DeviceUpdated`. Equal metadata produces no change; null does not erase a successful value. - Changes are ordered as all removals, then all additions, then all updates. Order within each group is not a public sorting guarantee. The revision increases once per applied scan, even if its diff is empty. All changes from that scan share the revision. Metadata lives on retained mutable device objects; a revision does not freeze it. Diffing and metadata refresh occur outside the feed gate, so atomic publication is a membership/change boundary, not transactional isolation of device properties. `DeviceInfo` scalar fields in a returned value survive snapshot replacement. Its `ChallengeResponseTimeout` memory currently aliases an input TLV, however, so read-only metadata is not a general independent-storage or post-disposal stability guarantee. See [cached metadata](../usage/device-discovery.md#cached-device-metadata). ## Publication and subscription Only the monitor loop calls `DeviceChangeFeed.Apply`. It computes the diff outside the gate, then under one short lock replaces the membership dictionary, advances the revision, and enqueues the complete ordered change list to every registered subscription. Published dictionaries are not mutated. No consumer code or logging runs under the gate; channel continuations are asynchronous. On the first `MoveNextAsync`, `Subscribe` captures the dictionary and revision and registers the subscriber under that same gate. Outside it, the iterator emits one `DeviceAdded` per captured member, one `SnapshotComplete` at the captured revision (even if empty), then reads its live tail. Capture and registration cannot miss an intervening publication. Replay itself uses no buffer capacity, but changes arriving during replay can fill the live buffer. Do not prepend an independent snapshot or Find call. Each subscriber has a 256-change buffer. Publication uses `TryWrite`, never waits for a consumer, and faults only the overflowing subscription with `InvalidOperationException` rather than dropping changes. Recovery clears the consumer projection and re-enumerates the same monitor. Cancellation or disposing an enumeration unregisters only that subscription. `Fault` records a terminal error and faults current subscriptions with a wrapped `InvalidOperationException`; new subscriptions see that failure until `Complete` is reached. `Complete` ends remaining healthy subscriptions normally and makes later enumerations end empty. It does not erase a channel error already set by terminal failure or overflow: those existing subscriptions retain their error after any captured replay and buffered history drain. ## Why listeners are hints, not truth All transports use `IDeviceChangeListener.Changed`, a payload-less callback. Set it before `Start` and check `Status` afterward. Never stop or dispose a listener inside its callback: native shutdown may wait for that callback. Platform-specific HID diagnostics remain internal Trace logging, not public arrival/removal payloads. Unknown removals still request reconciliation. One physical key can expose several interfaces, notifications can be duplicated/coalesced, and native events need not identify the physical key. Only discovery plus the snapshot diff determines public membership changes. Windows HID uses configuration-manager notifications, macOS uses IOKit callbacks, Linux uses udev, and the desktop smart-card listener uses PC/SC status changes. `HotplugSignals` tries each listener in turn. A startup exception or status other than `Started` is logged, followed by attempts to clear that listener's callback, stop it, and dispose it. Cleanup exceptions are caught and logged so later attempts can continue, provided logging itself returns. A throwing logger can interrupt startup or cleanup and prevent subsequent listener attempts. If construction completes without listeners, interval scans still run. Unavailable services may enumerate empty; this is best-effort partial discovery. ## Monitor lifecycle and disposal Creation starts listeners, launches the loop, and awaits its first publication. Empty success is ready. A failed first scan prevents successful creation. If the first-publication wait fails or is canceled, the factory awaits disposal of the constructed monitor before rethrowing. A cleanup exception can replace the earlier failure; this path does not guarantee original-error preservation or completion of every cleanup stage. The creation token is independent of the monitor lifetime after return. Later scan/publication exceptions are logged and retried on the next trigger. Discovery failures before publication retain the last membership. Unexpected failures outside that retry path fault the feed before best-effort diagnostic logging. A new subscription does not restart a failed monitor: dispose and create a new instance. There is no pause, restart, manual rescan, interval replacement, or monitor generation. `DisposeAsync` caches one disposal task. Its ordered cleanup path is: 1. Attempt to clear listener callbacks, then stop listeners, then dispose listeners through the best-effort cleanup helper, before completing the signal channel. 2. Cancel the lifetime token and await the actual scan loop, including any in-flight scan/publication. 3. Dispose the lifetime token source and retire discovery. 4. Complete the change feed. Each later stage depends on preceding calls returning. In particular, listener teardown runs before loop cancellation; a logger exception during listener cleanup can interrupt its loops or signal-channel completion and prevent cancellation, loop join, discovery retirement, and feed completion. Diagnostic logging after feed completion can also fault disposal even though the earlier stages ran. The loop-await stage has no disposal timeout or fallback that abandons its wait. In-flight scan waits are bounded by the discovery budgets; listener cleanup and total disposal are not a hard wall-clock promise. No producer can publish after feed completion because reaching that stage follows the loop's exit. Caller-owned connections and sessions retain their own lifetimes. Concurrent `WatchAsync` enumerations are supported, and `DisposeAsync` may overlap them. When cleanup reaches feed completion, healthy uncanceled streams can drain and end normally; an existing terminal-failure or overflow error remains observable on its subscription. Later enumerations end empty. `DisposeAsync` must not be called concurrently with itself. Applications that want consumers to observe a final state before shutdown do so on their own terms; disposal does not wait for consumers. ### Finder evidence epochs are not monitor generations Hotplug invalidation atomically replaces the whole identity/metadata evidence epoch and retires its read scope, even when only one transport signalled. Old native completion can write only into unreachable old caches; retaining sibling evidence could mix two physical keys. Scan-observed absence also evicts evidence. Without either hint or observed absence, same-interface substitution can remain unknowable. Read-scope retirement cancels queued admission and prevents later opens. Already-open reads retain actual worker admission and registry leases until native teardown. Sibling admission, same-product serialization, and unknown-product atomic reservation remain; a pending unknown-product request reserves no gates. Neither a wait budget nor scope retirement proves native release. See [native discovery scheduling](device-discovery-guarantees.md#native-discovery-scheduling). `SnapshotDiffTests` pins retention/replacement and metadata changes; `DeviceChangeFeedTests` pins replay, ordering, revisions, overflow, and termination. Monitor, scheduler, and hotplug tests cover initialization, sequential scans, timing, fallback, and disposal; enumeration-budget tests cover partial results and late work.
